claim: xrRNA1 is necessary and sufficient for efficient binding of FMRP, FXR1, and FXR2 to ZIKV 3' UTR.
source: As expected, the complete 3′ UTR interacted with FMRP, FXR1 and FXR2 (Figure 1, lane 1). Deletion of xrRNA1 dramatically reduced interaction with all three proteins (lane 2) and deletion of xrRNA1 and 2 eliminated detectable binding. Additionally, xrRNA1 alone was sufficient to bind FMRP, FXR1 and FXR2 (lane 4). These data indicate that xrRNA1 is necessary and sufficient for efficient binding to these proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from RNA affinity chromatography experiments using deletion mutants of the ZIKV 3' UTR shown in Figure 1.

claim: FMRP interacts with both ZIKV genomic RNA and sfRNA in infected HeLa cells, with preferential binding to sfRNA.
source: HeLa cells were infected with Dakar 41525 (ZIKV-Dakar), Cambodia FSS13025 (ZIKV-Cambodia) or PRVABC59 (ZIKV-Puerto Rico) strains, cell lysates were collected and FMRP was immunoprecipitated. Total RNA interacting with FMRP was isolated and the presence of ZIKV RNAs was detected by NB using a DNA probe that hybridizes to the ZIKV 3′ UTR. Both ZIKV sfRNA and viral genome co-precipitated with anti-FMRP but not control IgG (Figure 2A) for all three virus strains. Interestingly, quantification of sfRNA and genomic RNA signals indicated that FMRP preferentially interacts with the ZIKV sfRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation followed by northern blot analysis showing co-precipitation of viral RNAs with FMRP and quantification showing preferential sfRNA binding.

claim: FMRP interacts with ZIKV RNA in testes of infected A129 mice, with preferential binding to sfRNA.
source: We determined whether or not the interaction of FMRP with ZIKV RNA occurs in testes of infected mice. We selected testes for analysis because this tissue exhibits relatively high viral load in the A129 mouse model (IFNAR1 knockout) of ZIKV infection (Dowall et al., 2016; Rossi et al., 2016). FMRP was subjected to IP from testes lysates of mice infected with ZIKV-Cambodia for 6 days and RT-qPCR was used to measure co-precipitating viral RNA using qPCR assays targeting the viral genome exclusively or both the genome and sfRNA (Figure 2D). We observed enrichment of viral genomes by ~2 fold for FMRP IP compared to the negative control. Importantly, the enrichment was nearly twice as robust when using a qPCR assay that detects both genomes and the sfRNA. These results validate the interaction of FMRP with ZIKV RNA in vivo and, as observed in infected cultured cells, indicate preferential binding of FMRP to the ZIKV sfRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from FMRP immunoprecipitation experiments in infected mouse testes showing differential enrichment of viral genome versus genome plus sfRNA.

claim: FMRP knockdown increases ZIKV-Dakar infection rates by 2- to 5-fold in HeLa cells.
source: Forty-eight hours post-infection with ZIKV-Dakar at low MOI (0.01), we measured viral titers using plaque assay and rate of infection by flow cytometry. Both viral titers and rate of infection were increased by 2- to 5-fold due to FMRP KD (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by plaque assay and flow cytometry data showing increased viral titers and infection rates in FMRP knockdown cells.

claim: FMRP knockdown enhances infection with Asian ZIKV strains (ZIKV-Cambodia and ZIKV-Puerto Rico) but does not impact DENV-2 infection.
source: Moreover, we observed that FMRP KD enhanced infection with Asian strains (ZIKV-Cambodia and ZIKV-Puerto Rico) to different extents, but did not impact infection by DENV-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing infection rates in FMRP knockdown versus control cells for multiple virus strains.

claim: FXR1 knockdown slightly increases ZIKV infection rate while FXR2 knockdown significantly reduces infection.
source: We additionally tested the effect of FXR1 and FXR2 knockdown on ZIKV infection. We observed a slight increase in virus infection rate for FXR1 depletion while FXR2 knockdown significantly reduced infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing differential effects of FXR1 and FXR2 knockdown on ZIKV infection rates.

claim: FMRP depletion results in a 4-fold increase in ZIKV NanoLuc signal at 3.5 hours post-infection, indicating increased viral translation.
source: The Nanoluc signal observed in control cells was well above that detected in the CHX-treated control at 3.5 hr post infection (hpi) indicating measurable viral protein synthesis at this early time point. Importantly, we observed a 4-fold increase in NanoLuc signal in FMRP depleted cells (siFMR1) compared to control siRNA transfected cells, suggesting that FMRP depletion results in increased of ZIKV translation (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data from cells infected with NanoLuc-expressing ZIKV reporter virus.

claim: FMRP depletion increases ZIKV translation efficiency by 3.5-fold in both the absence and presence of the RNA replication inhibitor NITD008.
source: Similar effects were observed in the presence of NITD008, a potent inhibitor of the flaviviral NS5 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Deng et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2009), ruling out a possible contribution of RNA replication to the increased luciferase signal in FMRP KD cells (Figure 4A and B). Consistent with this, we did not observe significant differences in viral RNA accumulation between control and FMRP KD cells in the absence or presence of NITD008 (Figure 4C). Finally, we calculated a 3.5-fold increase of ZIKV translation efficiency (NanoLuc levels normalized to ZIKV RNA) in FMRP KD cells compared to the negative control in both the absence and presence of NITD008 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data normalized to viral RNA levels, demonstrating increased translation efficiency independent of RNA replication.

claim: Δ10 ZIKV has a defect in sfRNA accumulation compared to WT ZIKV, with an sfRNA/gRNA ratio of 0.6 versus 2.7.
source: We first asked whether Δ10 ZIKV is deficient in sfRNA production. Analysis of viral RNA from infected HeLa cells demonstrated that Δ10 ZIKV has a defect in sfRNA accumulation. An sfRNA/gRNA ratio of 2.7 was observed in WT ZIKV infected cells but the ratio was only 0.6 in Δ10 ZIKV infected cells. These results suggest that Δ10 ZIKV is attenuated, as least in part, through loss of sfRNA accumulation caused by the 10-nt deletion (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot analysis and densitometry quantification of sfRNA and genomic RNA levels in infected cells.

claim: FMRP knockdown disproportionately enhances Δ10 ZIKV infection compared to WT ZIKV, with approximately 5-fold versus 3-fold increases in infection rate.
source: We observed that Δ10 ZIKV infection rate in HeLa cells is reduced compared to WT ZIKV under negative control conditions (~11% vs~25% infected cells) and, importantly, FMRP KD disproportionately enhanced Δ10 ZIKV infection rate (Figure 5C): whereas WT virus was enhanced by approximately 3-fold, the infection rate for Δ10 ZIKV rose by nearly 5-fold (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing infection rates of WT and Δ10 ZIKV in control versus FMRP knockdown cells.

claim: WT ZIKV infection increases FXR2 protein levels by 2.7-fold in HeLa cells, while Δ10 ZIKV infection does not significantly increase FXR2 levels.
source: First, we analyzed expression levels of FXR2 by WB in HeLa cells infected with WT ZIKV and Δ10 ZIKV. In order to achieve similar infection rates for the two viruses, cells were infected at MOI of 3 for WT ZIKV and MOI of 4.5 for the mutant virus. Interestingly, these experiments revealed a 2.7-fold-increase of FXR2 protein levels in cells infected with WT ZIKV (Figure 6A and B). Although Δ10 ZIKV infection also increased the mean level of FXR2, this effect was not statistically significant (p=0.277) compared to uninfected cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis and densitometry quantification of FXR2 protein levels in infected versus uninfected cells.

claim: WT ZIKV infection increases FXR2 mean fluorescence intensity by 2-fold while Δ10 ZIKV increases it by 1.5-fold as measured by flow cytometry.
source: In parallel, we measured the expression of FXR2 by flow cytometry in ZIKV-infected cells using a double staining protocol. Figure 6C shows the distributions of the cells based on infection with either WT ZIKV or Δ10 ZIKV, indicating similar levels of infection for both viruses (~86% for WT and ~90% for Δ10 ZIKV). FXR2 mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was enhanced by WT virus and, to a lesser extent, by the Δ10 ZIKV mutant. Quantitatively, there was a two-fold increase of FXR2 MFI in WT ZIKV infected cells and a 1.5-fold increase for Δ10 ZIKV compared to uninfected cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring FXR2 protein expression in infected cells.

claim: Δ10 ZIKV infection causes FXR2 to redistribute into discrete cytoplasmic puncta, which also occurs at reduced frequency in WT ZIKV-infected cells.
source: We also conducted IF microscopy analysis and observed FXR2 accumulation specifically in ZIKV-infected cells (Figure 6E). Interestingly, infection of cells by Δ10 ZIKV caused FXR2 to redistribute into discrete cytoplasmic puncta which was also evident at reduced frequency in WT ZIKV-infected cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy images showing FXR2 localization patterns in infected cells.

claim: WT ZIKV infection increases TLN1 protein levels compared to uninfected and Δ10 ZIKV infected cells.
source: In addition to FXR2, we also observed elevated expression of TLN1 by WB in cells infected with WT ZIKV compared with uninfected and Δ10 ZIKV infected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis and densitometry quantification of TLN1 protein levels.

claim: Electroporation of intact ZIKV sfRNA results in modest but significant increases in FXR2 and BRD4 levels compared to DBSLIII control RNA.
source: In parallel, we analyzed the expression of the FMRP targets FXR2 and BRD4 by flow cytometry (Figure 7B to F). Compared to the DBSLIII RNA, electroporation of intact sfRNA resulted in modest, but highly significant, increases in both FXR2 and BRD4 levels. These results suggest expression of ZIKV sfRNA is sufficient to interfere with FMRP.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring FXR2 and BRD4 protein expression in cells electroporated with different RNA constructs.

claim: WT ZIKV infection in A129 mice increases FXR2 expression by 1.6-fold and PNPLA6 expression by 2.5-fold in testes compared to uninfected mice.
source: Male A129 mice were infected with WT (n = 4) or Δ10 ZIKV (n = 4) using 1 × 105 FFU. At 6 days post-infection, protein expression levels of FXR2 and PNPLA6 [a validated FMRP target (Ascano et al., 2012)] were measured in testes. In WT ZIKV-infected mice, we observed statistically significant increases in expression of both FXR2 (1.6-fold) and PNPLA6 (2.5-fold) compared to uninfected mice (Figure 8A,C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis and densitometry quantification of FXR2 and PNPLA6 protein levels in mouse testes.

claim: Δ10 ZIKV infection in A129 mice does not significantly increase FXR2 and PNPLA6 expression levels in testes.
source: For Δ10 ZIKV-infected mice, expression levels of FXR2 and PNPLA6 were elevated to lesser extents, but these effects were not statistically significant.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis showing non-significant changes in protein levels.

claim: WT ZIKV exhibits higher viral genome burden than Δ10 ZIKV in infected mouse testes.
source: Measurements of viral genomes indicated a higher burden of infection for the WT virus than Δ10 ZIKV (Figure 8B) which may contribute to the differential effects on FXR2 and PNPLA6 levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data measuring viral genome levels in mouse testes.

claim: FMRP acts as a specific restriction factor for multiple ZIKV strains.
source: Together, these observations suggest that FMRP acts as a specific restriction factor for multiple ZIKV strains.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing FMRP knockdown enhances infection of different ZIKV strains but not DENV.

claim: FMRP inhibits ZIKV infection by reducing viral translation.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that FMRP inhibits ZIKV infection by reducing viral translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by NanoLuc reporter assays showing increased viral protein synthesis in FMRP knockdown cells without changes in viral RNA levels.

claim: ZIKV sfRNA antagonizes FMRP activity.
source: Together, these results suggest that sfRNA antagonizes FMRP and thus enhances ZIKV infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing differential sensitivity of WT versus Δ10 ZIKV (deficient in sfRNA) to FMRP knockdown.

claim: ZIKV sfRNA works as a 'sink' to saturate FMRP and prevent its repressive interactions with both viral RNA and cellular target mRNAs.
source: We speculate that ZIKV sfRNA works as a 'sink' to saturate FMRP and prevent its repressive interactions with both viral RNA and cellular target mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on preferential binding of FMRP to sfRNA and effects on FMRP target gene expression.

claim: FMRP is an intrinsic, direct-acting ZIKV restriction factor that interacts with ZIKV RNA and is counteracted by the sfRNA.
source: In this work we describe that FMRP is an intrinsic, direct-acting ZIKV restriction factor that interacts with ZIKV RNA and is counteracted by the sfRNA as it accumulates during infection.
evidence: The claim summarizes multiple experimental findings including binding assays, knockdown experiments, and differential effects of WT versus Δ10 ZIKV.

claim: ZIKV infection blocks the canonical activity of FMRP and increases the expression of FMRP target genes.
source: Additionally, we observed that ZIKV infection blocks the canonical activity of FMRP and increases the expression of FMRP target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and flow cytometry data showing increased expression of FMRP target proteins (FXR2, TLN1, BRD4, PNPLA6) in infected cells and mice.

claim: The ZIKV 3' UTR is highly structured and consists of four domains: xrRNA1, xrRNA2, the dumbbell (DB) and the 3' SL.
source: The ZIKV 3′ UTR is highly structured and consists of four domains: xrRNA1, xrRNA2, the dumbbell (DB) and the 3′ SL (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published structural characterization of the ZIKV 3' UTR.

claim: The ZIKV 3' UTR contains confirmed and predicted pseudoknot interactions located in xrRNA1 and xrRNA2 that are important for stalling XRN1 and accumulation of sfRNA species.
source: The ZIKV 3′ UTR contains confirmed and predicted pseudoknot interactions located in xrRNA1 and xrRNA2, respectively. These pseudoknots are important for stalling of the cellular 5′ to 3′ exonuclease, XRN1, and accumulation of at least two sfRNA species (sfRNA1 and sfRNA2) (Akiyama et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on ZIKV sfRNA structure and function.

claim: DENV sfRNA interacts with stress granule associated proteins G3BP1, G3BP2 and CAPRIN1 and the ubiquitin ligase TRIM25 to dampen innate immune responses.
source: The DENV sfRNA has been shown to interact with stress granule associated proteins G3BP1, G3BP2 and CAPRIN1 and the ubiquitin ligase TRIM25 to dampen innate immune responses (Bidet et al., 2014; Manokaran et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on DENV sfRNA interactions.

claim: DENV-2 and KUNV sfRNAs inhibit XRN1 activity, leading to accumulation of uncapped transcripts and disruption of mRNA homeostasis.
source: Similarly, Moon et al reported that DENV-2 and KUNV sfRNAs inhibited XRN1 activity, leading to accumulation of uncapped transcripts in infected cells and disruption of mRNA homeostasis that could potentially deregulate antiviral responses (Moon et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on flavivirus sfRNA effects on XRN1.

claim: Musashi-1 (MSI1) is required for efficient ZIKV infection and interacts with viral genomes, and ZIKV infection disrupts MSI1 activity.
source: Regarding ZIKV, Musashi-1 (MSI1) was reported to be required for efficient infection and interact with viral genomes; additionally, ZIKV infection disrupted the activity of MSI1 (33).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on MSI1 and ZIKV.

claim: ZIKV is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that is closely related to dengue (DENV) and yellow fever viruses (YFV).
source: Zika virus (ZIKV) is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that is closely related to dengue (DENV) and yellow fever viruses (YFV).
evidence: The claim represents established scientific knowledge about ZIKV classification.

claim: There are three ZIKV genotypes: one from Asia and two from Africa (East and West African).
source: There are three ZIKV genotypes: one from Asia, which has caused the recent pandemic in the Americas, and two from Africa (East and West African) (Lanciotti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published phylogenetic analysis of ZIKV strains.

claim: ZIKV infection is characterized by fever, arthralgia and conjunctivitis.
source: ZIKV infection is characterized by fever, arthralgia and conjunctivitis (Goeijenbier et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published clinical descriptions of ZIKV infection.

claim: Only 14 ZIKV cases were reported prior to 2007.
source: ZIKV infection is characterized by fever, arthralgia and conjunctivitis (Goeijenbier et al., 2016) and was considered an exceedingly rare human infection since only 14 cases were reported prior to 2007 (Faye et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published epidemiological data.

claim: The first ZIKV outbreak caused by an Asian lineage was reported in Micronesia in 2007, followed by epidemics in French Polynesia in 2013 and the pandemic in the Americas (2015-2016).
source: In 2007, the first ZIKV outbreak caused by an Asian lineage was reported in Micronesia, followed by epidemics in French Polynesia in 2013 and the recent pandemic (2015–2016) in the Americas (Weaver et al., 2016; Aliota et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published epidemiological reports.

claim: It has been estimated that 1.5 million ZIKV cases occurred in Brazil and more than 25,000 cases in Colombia during the pandemic period.
source: During this period, it has been estimated that 1.5 million cases occurred in Brazil and more than 25,000 cases in Colombia (Focosi et al., 2016; Samarasekera and Triunfol, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published epidemiological estimates.

claim: As of January 2018, ZIKV was widely distributed in 50 countries in the Americas.
source: As of January 2018, the virus was widely distributed in 50 countries in the Americas (PAHO/WHO, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to PAHO/WHO epidemiological data.

claim: ZIKV has maternal-fetal and sexual modes of transmission.
source: The public health concern about Zika has been primarily driven by its maternal-fetal (Brasil et al., 2016a; Yockey et al., 2016; Driggers et al., 2016) and sexual modes of transmission (Deckard et al., 2016; Davidson et al., 2016; Hills et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published reports of ZIKV transmission routes.

claim: ZIKV is associated with congenital abnormalities, especially microcephaly, and Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults.
source: The public health concern about Zika has been primarily driven by its maternal-fetal (Brasil et al., 2016a; Yockey et al., 2016; Driggers et al., 2016) and sexual modes of transmission (Deckard et al., 2016; Davidson et al., 2016; Hills et al., 2016) as well as its association with congenital abnormalities, especially microcephaly, and Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults (Krauer et al., 2017; Martines et al., 2016; Miner et al., 2016; Brasil et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published clinical and epidemiological studies.

claim: The ZIKV life-cycle starts with virus attachment and receptor-mediated endocytosis.
source: The ZIKV life-cycle starts with virus attachment and receptor-mediated endocytosis (Hamel et al., 2015; Meertens et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on ZIKV entry mechanisms.

claim: Upon endosome acidification, the ZIKV envelope fuses with the endosomal membrane, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm for uncoating and initial viral translation at the cytosolic surface of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Upon endosome acidification, the viral envelope fuses with the endosomal membrane, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm for uncoating and initial viral translation at the cytosolic surface of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about flavivirus replication cycles.

claim: ZIKV translation produces a single polyprotein that is cleaved into 10 mature proteins: three structural proteins (C, prM, E) and seven non-structural proteins (NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B, NS5).
source: Translation produces a single polyprotein that is cleaved co- and post-translationally by cellular and viral proteases into 10 mature proteins: three structural proteins forming the virion (capsid, C; pre-membrane, prM; and envelope, E) and seven non-structural proteins (NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B and NS5) required for viral replication and inhibition of host defense mechanisms (Campos et al., 2017; Barrows et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published reviews of flavivirus molecular biology.

claim: Replication of ZIKV RNA and assembly of viral particles occur in close association with rearranged ER membranes.
source: Replication of ZIKV RNA and assembly of viral particles occur in close association with rearranged ER membranes (Rossignol et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published ultrastructural studies of ZIKV replication.

claim: Assembled ZIKV virions are transported through the secretory pathway, where furin protease cleaves prM into M, resulting in mature virions that are secreted.
source: Assembled virions are transported through the secretory pathway, where the furin protease cleaves prM into and M, resulting in mature virions that are secreted into the extracellular space (Hasan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on flavivirus maturation.

claim: The flaviviral genome contains 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTR) that are essential for genome cyclization and initiation of RNA synthesis.
source: The flaviviral genome contains 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions (UTR) that are essential for genome cyclization and initiation of RNA synthesis (Filomatori et al., 2006; Alvarez et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on flavivirus RNA structure and function.

claim: DDX6 interacts specifically with the ZIKV dumbbell region in contrast to FMRP.
source: DDX6 interacted specifically with the ZIKV dumbbell region in contrast to FMRP.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from RNA affinity chromatography experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: PTB and G3BP1 did not strongly interact with ZIKV 3' UTR.
source: Interestingly, PTB and G3BP1, which were previously reported to interact with the DENV 3′ UTR (Bidet et al., 2014; De Nova-Ocampo et al., 2002), did not strongly interact with ZIKV 3′ UTR (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from RNA affinity chromatography experiments and citations to previous work on DENV.

claim: Viral genomes and sfRNA minimally co-precipitated with PTB and enrichment was much weaker than that for FMRP RIP.
source: We additionally performed RIP with anti-PTB and isotype control antibodies and showed that viral genomes and sfRNA minimally co-precipitated with PTB and enrichment was much weaker than that for FMRP RIP (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data from RNA immunoprecipitation experiments comparing FMRP and PTB.

claim: Viral RNAs did not degrade during the RIP procedure.
source: We also analyzed the integrity of unbound viral RNAs present in supernatants after RIP. This analysis revealed that viral RNAs did not degrade during the RIP procedure (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot analysis of supernatant fractions from RIP experiments.

claim: A129 mice (IFNAR1 knockout) exhibit relatively high viral load in testes during ZIKV infection.
source: We selected testes for analysis because this tissue exhibits relatively high viral load in the A129 mouse model (IFNAR1 knockout) of ZIKV infection (Dowall et al., 2016; Rossi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies characterizing ZIKV infection in A129 mice.

claim: FMRP knockdown increases ZIKV NS4B and NS2B protein levels in cells infected at MOIs of 1 and 5.
source: WB analysis revealed increased NS4B and NS2B protein levels in FMRP KD cells infected with ZIKV at MOIs of 1 and 5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis and densitometry quantification of viral proteins.

claim: During a single ZIKV replication cycle, the absence of FMRP significantly increases both the rate of infection and the level of viral protein accumulation per cell.
source: Together, these data indicate that during a single ZIKV replication cycle, the absence of FMRP significantly increases both the rate of infection and the level of viral protein accumulation per cell.
evidence: The claim is inferred from flow cytometry and western blot data showing increased infection rates and viral protein levels in FMRP knockdown cells.

claim: FMRP is known to be a repressor of cellular mRNA translation.
source: Because FMRP is known to be a repressor of cellular mRNA translation (Zalfa et al., 2003; Laggerbauer et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on FMRP function.

claim: FMRP depletion does not significantly affect viral RNA accumulation in the absence or presence of NITD008.
source: Consistent with this, we did not observe significant differences in viral RNA accumulation between control and FMRP KD cells in the absence or presence of NITD008 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data measuring viral RNA levels in control versus FMRP knockdown cells.

claim: Δ10 ZIKV contains a 10-nt deletion within the 3' UTR DB structure and is highly attenuated in mice and non-human primates.
source: For this purpose, we analyzed a ZIKV mutant (Δ10 ZIKV) that contains a 10-nt deletion within the 3′ UTR DB structure and is highly attenuated in mice and non-human primates (Shan et al., 2017a; Shan et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published characterization of the Δ10 ZIKV vaccine candidate.

claim: FMRP knockdown increases NS2B and NS4B protein levels more in Δ10 ZIKV infected cells than in WT ZIKV infected cells.
source: Additionally, similar effects were observed on levels of cell-associated ZIKV NS2B and NS4B proteins (Figure 5E to G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis showing differential effects of FMRP knockdown on viral protein levels for WT versus Δ10 ZIKV.

claim: FXR2, TLN1 and BRD4 are genuine FMRP targets in HeLa cells.
source: Protein levels of FXR2, TLN1 and BRD4 increased after transfection of siRNA targeting FMRP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the mRNAs encoding these proteins are genuine FMRP targets in HeLa cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing increased protein levels upon FMRP knockdown.

claim: FMRP may have cell-type specific effects on target gene expression.
source: The remaining proteins were either undetectable (ARC) or were unaffected (RAC1, Rho A, PNPLA6, KDM5C, TSC2, SOD1) which suggests that FMRP may have cell-type specific effects (Ascano et al., 2012; Darnell and Klann, 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from differential effects on known FMRP targets in HeLa cells and supported by citations to published work on FMRP target specificity.

claim: FXR2 has been previously reported to concentrate in stress granules.
source: FXR2 has been previously reported to concentrate in stress granules (Gonçalves et al., 2011), suggesting that infection with the attenuated virus may induce formation of stress granules more efficiently than WT ZIKV.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on FXR2 localization and used to interpret immunofluorescence observations.

claim: ZIKV infection causes cleavage of BRD4, producing a ~175 kDa species.
source: Although the anti-BRD4 antibody used recognizes the largest known BRD4 isoform, we observed a second and faster migrating band of ~175 kDa that appeared only in ZIKV-infected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C). Since there are no annotated isoforms of this predicted mass, the data suggest that BRD4 is cleaved during ZIKV infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from western blot data showing a novel BRD4-reactive band only in infected cells.

claim: WT ZIKV infection increases total BRD4 expression (sum of 204 kDa and 175 kDa species) by 1.6-fold.
source: We analyzed the sum of signals for both 204 kDa and 175 kDa BRD4 species and observed a 1.6-fold increase of BRD4 expression only in WT ZIKV infected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by densitometry analysis of western blot data.

claim: Three distinct sfRNA species (sfRNA1, sfRNA2, and sfRNA3) are produced during ZIKV infection.
source: We detected three distinct sfRNA species in infected cells that have been previously reported for ZIKV: sfRNA1, sfRNA2 and sfRNA3 (Figure 7A and B) (Filomatori et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data and citation to published characterization of ZIKV sfRNA species.

claim: Electroporated sfRNA is partially degraded although some intact sfRNA remains even at 48 hr post-electroporation.
source: Electroporated RNAs were partially degraded although some intact sfRNA remained even at 48 hr post-electroporation.
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot analysis of electroporated RNA stability shown in Figure 7.

claim: FMRP has high expression levels in brain, placenta and testes.
source: Our observations have implications for ZIKV pathogenesis in tissues with high expression of FMRP: brain, placenta and testes (Hinds et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published expression analysis of FMRP.

claim: Certain aspects of ZIKV neuropathogenesis may be explained by sfRNA-mediated FMRP inhibition, leading to inappropriate expression of FMRP target mRNAs.
source: Given the well-established role for FMRP in promoting neurodevelopment, it is tempting to speculate that certain aspects of ZIKV neuropathogenesis may be explained by sfRNA-mediated FMRP inhibition, leading to inappropriate expression of FMRP target mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning connecting FMRP's known role in neurodevelopment with observed effects of ZIKV on FMRP activity.

claim: Development of congenital Zika syndrome is likely multifactorial and microcephaly is unlikely to be solely the consequence of FMRP inhibition.
source: Development of congenital Zika syndrome is likely multifactorial and symptoms such as microcephaly, which is only one disease manifestation (Aliota et al., 2017), are unlikely to be the consequence of FMRP inhibition.
evidence: The claim represents cautious interpretation acknowledging the complexity of ZIKV pathogenesis.

claim: ZIKV interactions with FMRP might contribute to disease outcome.
source: Nevertheless, our findings warrant further research into how ZIKV interactions with FMRP might contribute to disease outcome.
evidence: The claim represents a conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis of FMRP CLIP-seq datasets identified WGGA (W = T/A) as the top sequence motif.
source: Bioinformatic analysis of FMRP CLIP-seq datasets identified WGGA (W = T/A) as the top sequence motif (Anderson et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published bioinformatic analysis of FMRP binding specificity.

claim: The WGGA motif is found at six sites in the ZIKV 3' UTR, each located in the dumbbell regions.
source: Bioinformatic analysis of FMRP CLIP-seq datasets identified WGGA (W = T/A) as the top sequence motif (Anderson et al., 2016) which is found at six sites in the ZIKV 3′ UTR, each of them located in the dumbbell regions.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of the ZIKV 3' UTR.

claim: The WGGA motifs in the ZIKV dumbbell regions do not mediate interaction with FMRP.
source: Our mapping experiments, however, showed that the dumbbells are dispensable for FMRP binding to ZIKV 3′UTR, suggesting that these WGGA motifs do not mediate interaction with FMRP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNA affinity chromatography experiments showing xrRNA1 is necessary and sufficient for FMRP binding.

claim: Darnell et al. identified a highly structured target for the FMRP KH2 domain containing a pseudoknot using in vitro RNA selection.
source: Interestingly, using in vitro RNA selection Darnell et al. identified a highly structured target for the FMRP KH2 domain containing a pseudoknot (Darnell et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on FMRP RNA-binding specificity.

claim: No FMRP target mRNA has been identified that contains the pseudoknot motif identified by Darnell et al.
source: To date, no FMRP target mRNA has been identified that contains this motif
evidence: The claim represents current knowledge about FMRP target identification.

claim: The ZIKV xrRNA1 folds into a complex structure containing several tertiary interactions.
source: but it is notable that the ZIKV xrRNA1, which is required for FMRP binding in vitro, folds into a complex structure containing several tertiary interactions (Akiyama et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published structural characterization of ZIKV xrRNA1.

claim: The artificial RNA identified by Darnell and colleagues may share similar three-dimensional structural features with the ZIKV sfRNA that allow high-affinity FMRP binding.
source: We speculate that the artificial RNA identified by Darnell and colleagues shares similar three-dimensional structural features with the sfRNA which allow it to bind FMRP with high affinity.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning connecting published FMRP binding data with observed ZIKV sfRNA binding.

claim: FMRP was previously identified as a DENV RNA-binding protein by RNA affinity chromatography.
source: It is not clear why DENV infection is immune to FMRP. It is possible that DENV eludes physical interaction with FMRP in infected cells or that ribosomes translating DENV RNA do not effectively recruit FMRP, which is thought to be a prerequisite for translational repression (Chen et al., 2014; Blackwell et al., 2010). Notably, FMRP was recently described as a proviral host factor for influenza A virus that promotes assembly of viral RNPs, and FXR proteins were shown to redundantly promote replication of specific alphaviruses (Zhou et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work identifying FMRP as a DENV-binding protein.

claim: DENV may elude physical interaction with FMRP in infected cells or ribosomes translating DENV RNA may not effectively recruit FMRP.
source: It is not clear why DENV infection is immune to FMRP. It is possible that DENV eludes physical interaction with FMRP in infected cells or that ribosomes translating DENV RNA do not effectively recruit FMRP, which is thought to be a prerequisite for translational repression (Chen et al., 2014; Blackwell et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning attempting to explain why DENV is not restricted by FMRP despite binding to it.

claim: FMRP is a proviral host factor for influenza A virus that promotes assembly of viral RNPs.
source: Notably, FMRP was recently described as a proviral host factor for influenza A virus that promotes assembly of viral RNPs, and FXR proteins were shown to redundantly promote replication of specific alphaviruses (Zhou et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on FMRP and influenza A virus.

claim: FXR proteins redundantly promote replication of specific alphaviruses.
source: Notably, FMRP was recently described as a proviral host factor for influenza A virus that promotes assembly of viral RNPs, and FXR proteins were shown to redundantly promote replication of specific alphaviruses (Zhou et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on FXR proteins and alphaviruses.

claim: Hirano et al. showed interaction of FMRP with the genomic RNA of Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV), accumulation of FMRP at sites of local TBEV replication, and that FMRP depletion reduces TBEV infection.
source: Hirano et al. showed interaction of FMRP with the genomic RNA of Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV), accumulation of FMRP at sites of local TBEV replication, and that FMRP depletion reduces TBEV infection (Hirano et al., 2017; Muto et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on FMRP and TBEV.

claim: FMRP can play a positive, negative or no role in infection, depending on viral species.
source: Thus, FMRP can play a positive, negative or no role in infection, depending on viral species.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple cited studies showing different roles of FMRP for different viruses.

claim: FMRP is widely expressed and has been characterized to repress translation of specific neuronal mRNAs.
source: FMRP is widely expressed and has been characterized to repress translation of specific neuronal mRNAs but the precise mechanism is unknown.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about FMRP expression and function.

claim: Drosophila FMRP (dFMRP) can bind directly to the ribosome in the absence of mRNA.
source: Chen et al. demonstrated that drosophila FMRP (dFMRP) can bind directly to the ribosome in the absence of mRNA (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published structural and biochemical studies.

claim: FMRP docks on the 80S ribosome using KH1/2 domains and simultaneously binds to mRNA via its RGG motif.
source: The authors proposed that FMRP docks on the 80S ribosome using KH1/2 domains and simultaneously binds to mRNA via its RGG motif.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published mechanistic model of FMRP function.

claim: The binding location of dFMRP on the ribosome suggests that it occludes recruitment of elongation factors and tRNA, leading to reversible ribosome stalling.
source: The binding location of dFMRP on the ribosome suggests that it occludes recruitment of elongation factors and tRNA, leading the ribosome reversibly stall as observed by Darnell et al. (Darnell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published mechanistic studies of FMRP-mediated translational repression.

claim: FMRP may bind the ZIKV genome within the viral open reading frame and cause elongating ribosomes to stall, leading to deficiency in viral protein synthesis.
source: Based on this proposed mechanism, we speculate that FMRP binds the ZIKV genome within the viral open reading frame and causes elongating ribosomes to stall, leading to a deficiency in viral protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning applying the known FMRP mechanism to ZIKV translation.

claim: FMRP interaction with the 3' UTR of the viral genome could lead to impaired translation.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that FMRP interaction with the 3′ UTR of the viral genome could lead to impaired translation.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning proposing an alternative mechanism for FMRP-mediated restriction.

claim: Changes in the expression of FMRP targets may indirectly contribute to enhanced ZIKV infection upon FMRP knockdown.
source: Finally, changes in the expression of FMRP targets may indirectly contribute to enhanced ZIKV infection upon FMRP knockdown. For example, the increase in FXR2 subsequent to FMRP depletion could positively impact ZIKV infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning considering indirect effects of FMRP knockdown on ZIKV infection.

claim: ZIKV sfRNA may prevent stress granule formation.
source: Interestingly, infection of cells by Δ10 ZIKV caused FXR2 to redistribute into discrete cytoplasmic puncta which was also evident at reduced frequency in WT ZIKV-infected cells. FXR2 has been previously reported to concentrate in stress granules (Gonçalves et al., 2011), suggesting that infection with the attenuated virus may induce formation of stress granules more efficiently than WT ZIKV.
evidence: The claim is inferred from differential FXR2 localization patterns in WT versus Δ10 ZIKV infected cells and knowledge of FXR2 stress granule localization.

claim: Very low stress granule formation occurs in flavivirus infected cells.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that show very low SG formation in flavivirus infected cells (Bidet et al., 2014; Emara and Brinton, 2007; Ruggieri et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on stress granule formation during flavivirus infection.

claim: ZIKV sfRNA is reminiscent of the DENV sfRNA role as a molecular sink for proteins involved in interferon responses.
source: This is reminiscent of recently described roles for the DENV sfRNA as a molecular sink for proteins involved in interferon responses (G3BP1, G3BP2, CAPRIN1, TRIM25) (Bidet et al., 2014; Manokaran et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim draws an analogy between ZIKV and DENV sfRNA functions based on cited literature.

claim: YTHDF1-3 proteins bind methylated RNA and regulate stability, interact with ZIKV RNA and inhibit infection.
source: For flaviviruses, a few intrinsic anti-viral factors have been described: YTHDF1-3 proteins that bind methylated RNA and regulate stability, were reported to interact with ZIKV RNA and inhibit infection (Lichinchi et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on YTHDF proteins and ZIKV.

claim: YB-1 and QKI bind to the DENV 3' UTR and repress DENV RNA translation.
source: YB-1 and QKI bind to the DENV 3′ UTR and repress DENV RNA translation (Liao et al., 2018; Paranjape and Harris, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on DENV restriction factors.

claim: FBP1 blocks translation of JEV through interacting with untranslated regions of JEV RNA.
source: similarly, FBP1 blocks translation of JEV through interacting with untranslated regions of JEV RNA (Chien et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on JEV restriction factors.

claim: The association of intrinsic antiviral factors with flaviviral genomes and their functional consequences have only been observed in cell culture and remain to be validated in vivo.
source: The association of these antiviral factors with the viral genome and their functional consequences have only been observed in cell culture and it remains to be seen whether or not these will be validated in vivo.
evidence: The claim represents a critical assessment of the current state of knowledge about flavivirus restriction factors.

claim: There are no reports that the intrinsic anti-viral function of previously described flavivirus restriction factors is counteracted by flaviviral factors.
source: Furthermore, there are no reports that the intrinsic anti-viral function of these proteins is counteracted by flaviviral factors.
evidence: The claim represents a knowledge gap in the field that the current work addresses.

claim: ZIKV pathogenesis may involve virus-mediated FMRP inhibition.
source: Finally, we present evidence implicating deregulation of FMRP activity in a mouse model of ZIKV infection, suggesting that ZIKV pathogenesis may involve virus-mediated FMRP inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from in vivo data showing upregulation of FMRP targets in infected mice.

claim: Interaction between ZIKV and FMRP has significant implications for the pathogenesis of ZIKV infections.
source: Together, our observations identify FMRP as a ZIKV restriction factor whose activity is antagonized by the sfRNA. Interaction between ZIKV and FMRP has significant implications for the pathogenesis of ZIKV infections.
evidence: The claim represents a broad conclusion about the significance of the findings.
